attacks.claim: The open-data export publishes ward, zip, birth_year, gender alongside ranking and created_at per poll, and the verified-resident data includes address-derived ward. Combined with timestamps and small per-ward/zip cells, individuals become re-identifiable and linkable across polls, and sensitive demographic attributes are made public under CC-BY with no retention limit or consent mechanism.
attacks.evidence: "one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export."

attacks.claim: Purchasing the county voter file and texting all ~142,000 registered voters with 4 automated SMS messages is a bulk unsolicited messaging campaign using personal contact data that residents did not provide to OurTown; the plan has no consent basis, no statement of how the numbers are protected or deleted, and treats STOP as the only control.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided)." / "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000)"

attacks.claim: Automated marketing-style SMS to purchased lists without prior express consent violates the TCPA (US) and carrier 10DLC rules; statutory damages run per message, so 142,000 recipients times 4 messages is a large exposure. Relying on Twilio's default STOP handling does not satisfy TCPA consent requirements.
attacks.evidence: "Load numbers into Twilio and send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000) with a link to the first poll, then 3 automated reminders over 10 days." / "Reply STOP handled by Twilio's default opt-out."

attacks.claim: Voter-file data use is typically restricted by state law to election, political, or government purposes; using it to recruit app users for a nonprofit civic tool, and possibly to publish derived data, may violate the purchase terms and state voter-file statutes. No legal review is mentioned.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any review of the County Clerk's permitted-use terms or state voter-file statute before purchase

attacks.claim: Verified residents' address, birth_year, and gender are stored in the same schema as poll responses, and the plan says these are collected 'for jury-pool-style demographic balance reports' — a purpose not disclosed to residents here and not governed by a retention policy. Linking verified responses to this data is a linkability risk.
attacks.evidence: "Verified residents already have address, zip, birth_year, gender (collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports)."

attacks.claim: Device-fingerprint and IP-based limits are trivially evaded, and 'verified' is the only trust signal; a brigade can still flood unverified responses and the 'queued for review' path has no defined reviewer, SLA, or behavior for the live tally, so results can be skewed before review.
attacks.evidence: "Rate limit: 1 response per poll per device fingerprint + 1 per verified resident; unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review."

attacks.claim: Ward is self-selected for unverified users, so the per-ward results and IRV tallies can be arbitrarily manipulated and presented as neighborhood sentiment; the plan does not say whether unverified responses count in per-ward IRV outputs or how the 'verified' split is shown per ward.
attacks.evidence: "Unverified responses are accepted; ward is self-selected for unverified users"

attacks.claim: The survey shows only 9% want polls, yet the plan calls Ward Voice the 'centerpiece' and the 30% new-user and 6,000-response targets have no basis in the data; the success metric is unsupported and the 61%/44% top requests are not addressed.
attacks.evidence: "Polls on upcoming items — 9%" / "Ward Voice ... is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap."

attacks.claim: The build prioritizes a feature that 9% of surveyed residents requested while the top requests (member voting records with reasons, neighborhood alerts) are absent from the plan, so the team may deliver the wrong thing before budget hearings.
attacks.evidence: "See how my council member voted on each item, and their stated reason — 61%" vs. "Polls on upcoming items — 9%"; ABSENT from Section 2 and Timeline

attacks.claim: Once the SMS campaign and open-data CSV publish, they cannot be recalled; the plan has no kill switch, no staged rollout, and no rollback for the public data export.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: rollback or feature-flag plan; "weekly, public, CC-BY" export

attacks.claim: Load test targets 5k concurrent in week 5 with SMS blast to 142k numbers on launch; no queueing, Twilio rate-limit handling, or retry/backoff is specified, and the single-host self-hosted Django/Postgres has no capacity plan for the spike.
attacks.evidence: "load test (target 5k concurrent), launch" / ABSENT: rate-limit and retry design for the SMS pipeline

attacks.claim: SMS cost for ~142,000 recipients times up to 4 messages (~568,000 segments) is not budgeted; only the $400 file fee is stated.
attacks.evidence: "then 3 automated reminders over 10 days" / ABSENT: Twilio cost estimate

attacks.claim: Drag-based ranking is named as the primary input; no keyboard or screen-reader alternative is specified beyond a generic week-5 accessibility pass.
Twilio is a single external SMS dependency for the whole outreach channel, with no exit path described.
The per-minute IP rate limit and weekly CSV export do not describe behavior at 10x poll volume.
Five-week timeline for a 3-person team covering data model, two UIs, IRV, open data, PDF, SMS pipeline, and load test is tight with no contingency.
The 'Monday 07:00' staff email has no timezone and no failure alerting.
